title: Services and layered architecture
intro: A Spring Boot application becomes much easier to change when each class has one clear responsibility. In this lesson, you will separate HTTP handling, business logic and data access into controller, service and repository layers, then see how dependency injection makes the service easy to test.
body:
## Why not put everything in the controller?

Our first REST controller was intentionally simple. It received an HTTP request and returned a response. That is a good way to learn the basic Spring MVC flow, but a real application quickly needs more logic.

~~~diagram
{"type": "layers", "title": "Each layer has one job", "layers": [{"label": "Controller", "sub": "HTTP in, HTTP out", "items": ["@RestController", "DTO", "@Valid", "status codes"]}, {"label": "Service", "sub": "business rules", "items": ["@Service", "@Transactional", "domain exceptions"], "highlight": true}, {"label": "Repository", "sub": "data access", "items": ["JpaRepository", "queries"]}, {"label": "Database", "items": ["PostgreSQL"]}]}
~~~

Imagine putting all of this into `TaskController`:

- reading HTTP parameters
- validating request data
- checking whether a task already exists
- deciding whether a task can be completed
- calculating business rules
- loading data from PostgreSQL
- saving entities
- converting entities into DTOs
- choosing HTTP status codes

The controller would become large and difficult to test.

The solution is **layered architecture**. Instead of making one class responsible for everything, we separate the application into layers with clear responsibilities.

The basic flow is:

~~~text
HTTP request
    ↓
Controller
    ↓
Service
    ↓
Repository
    ↓
Database
~~~

Each layer answers a different question.

## The controller layer

The controller is the HTTP boundary of the application.

Its job is to understand HTTP-specific concepts such as:

- URL paths
- HTTP methods
- path variables
- query parameters
- request bodies
- response status codes
- HTTP headers

For example:

~~~java
@PostMapping
public ResponseEntity<TaskResponse> create(
    @Valid @RequestBody CreateTaskRequest request
) {
    Task task = taskService.create(request.title());

    TaskResponse response = taskMapper.toResponse(task);

    return ResponseEntity
        .created(URI.create("/api/tasks/" + task.id()))
        .body(response);
}
~~~

The controller does not need to know how PostgreSQL works. It also should not decide whether a task with the same title already exists.

Those are responsibilities of other layers.

## The service layer

The service contains **application and business logic**.

For our task manager, examples include:

- a task title must be unique
- completing an already completed task is not allowed
- completing a missing task should produce a not-found error
- creating a task should start with `done = false`

A service might look like:

~~~java
@Service
public class TaskService {

    private final TaskRepository repository;

    public TaskService(TaskRepository repository) {
        this.repository = repository;
    }

    public Task create(String title) {
        if (repository.existsByTitleIgnoreCase(title)) {
            throw new ConflictException("Task already exists");
        }

        Task task = new Task();
        task.setTitle(title.trim());
        task.setDone(false);

        return repository.save(task);
    }
}
~~~

`@Service` tells Spring that this class is an application component that should be managed by the Spring container.

The important design principle is that **business rules belong in the service rather than in the controller**.

That makes the rules reusable. A REST controller, scheduled job or future command-line interface can all use the same service instead of duplicating the rules.

## The repository layer

The repository is responsible for data access.

It answers questions such as:

- How do I find a task by ID?
- How do I find all tasks?
- How do I save a task?
- Does a task with this title already exist?

With Spring Data JPA, you will eventually write something like:

~~~java
@Repository
public interface TaskRepository extends JpaRepository<TaskEntity, Long> {
    boolean existsByTitleIgnoreCase(String title);
}
~~~

`@Repository` identifies a repository component. Spring Data can also create the implementation automatically when you use a Spring Data repository interface.

The repository should not decide application policy. For example, the repository can answer whether a task exists, but the service decides what that means for the operation currently being performed.

## Interfaces create boundaries

An interface describes what a component can do without specifying how it does it.

For example:

~~~java
public interface TaskRepository {
    Optional<Task> findById(Long id);
    List<Task> findAll();
    Task save(Task task);
}
~~~

The service can depend on this contract rather than a concrete database implementation.

This is useful for both architecture and testing.

The service says:

~~~text
I need something that can find and save tasks.
~~~

It does not need to say:

~~~text
I specifically need PostgreSQL and this exact database implementation.
~~~

In the production application, Spring Data JPA can provide the real implementation. In a unit test, a tiny fake implementation can provide predictable data.

## Dependency injection

A service needs a repository. One approach would be to construct the repository manually inside the service, but that tightly couples the classes.

~~~diagram
{"type": "flow", "title": "Spring wires the layers for you", "caption": "You declare what a class needs in its constructor; the container creates the objects and passes them in.", "nodes": [{"id": "ctx", "label": "ApplicationContext", "sub": "creates every bean once", "kind": "service", "highlight": true}, {"id": "r", "label": "TaskRepository"}, {"id": "s", "label": "TaskService", "sub": "(TaskRepository repo)"}, {"id": "c", "label": "TaskController", "sub": "(TaskService service)"}], "edges": [{"from": "ctx", "to": "r", "label": "new"}, {"from": "r", "to": "s", "label": "injected"}, {"from": "s", "to": "c", "label": "injected"}]}
~~~

Spring uses **dependency injection** to provide objects with the dependencies they need.

The preferred style in our application is constructor injection:

~~~java
@Service
public class TaskService {

    private final TaskRepository repository;

    public TaskService(TaskRepository repository) {
        this.repository = repository;
    }
}
~~~

Spring sees that `TaskService` needs a `TaskRepository` and supplies an appropriate implementation when it creates the service.

The dependency is therefore explicit: you can look at the constructor and immediately see what the class requires.

### Why constructor injection?

Constructor injection has several advantages.

First, required dependencies cannot be forgotten when the object is created.

Second, the field can be `final`, which communicates that the dependency does not change after construction.

Third, the class is easy to create in a unit test without starting Spring.

For example:

~~~java
TaskRepository fakeRepository = new FakeTaskRepository();
TaskService service = new TaskService(fakeRepository);
~~~

You can now test the service directly.

### Why not field injection?

You may see code like this:

~~~java
@Autowired
private TaskRepository repository;
~~~

This is called **field injection**. Spring puts the dependency directly into the field.

It works, but it hides the class's required dependencies and makes ordinary unit tests less convenient because the object cannot be correctly constructed simply with `new TaskService(...)`.

For this course, use constructor injection for required dependencies.

## Interfaces for services too

You may sometimes see a service interface such as:

~~~java
public interface TaskService {
    Task create(String title);
}
~~~

with an implementation:

~~~java
@Service
public class TaskServiceImpl implements TaskService {
    // ...
}
~~~

Interfaces can be useful when you genuinely need multiple implementations or a stable abstraction between components.

However, do not create an interface for every class automatically. An interface should solve a real design problem, such as providing multiple implementations or making a boundary explicit.

Our repository is a natural interface because the service should not care whether data comes from PostgreSQL, an in-memory fake or another storage system.

## Keep business rules in the service

Consider completing a task.

The rule is:

1. Find the task.
2. If it does not exist, report not found.
3. If it is already done, report a conflict.
4. Otherwise mark it as done.
5. Save it.
6. Return the updated task.

This is business logic, so it belongs in the service.

~~~java
public Task complete(Long id) {
    Task task = repository.findById(id)
        .orElseThrow(() -> new TaskNotFoundException("Task not found"));

    if (task.isDone()) {
        throw new ConflictException("Task is already done");
    }

    task.setDone(true);
    return repository.save(task);
}
~~~

The controller should not reproduce this logic.

The controller's responsibility is closer to:

~~~java
@PatchMapping("/{id}/complete")
public TaskResponse complete(@PathVariable Long id) {
    return mapper.toResponse(taskService.complete(id));
}
~~~

The service contains the rule; the controller exposes it over HTTP.

## Mapping entities and DTOs

There are often three different representations of a piece of data:

~~~text
HTTP JSON
   ↕
DTO
   ↕
Entity
   ↕
Database
~~~

A **DTO (Data Transfer Object)** represents data crossing an application boundary. An **entity** represents data managed by the persistence layer.

For example:

~~~java
public record TaskResponse(
    Long id,
    String title,
    boolean done
) {}
~~~

Your database entity might contain additional persistence-specific fields:

~~~java
@Entity
public class TaskEntity {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue
    private Long id;

    private String title;
    private boolean done;
}
~~~

The API does not have to expose the entity directly.

A mapper converts between the representations:

~~~java
public TaskResponse toResponse(TaskEntity task) {
    return new TaskResponse(
        task.getId(),
        task.getTitle(),
        task.isDone()
    );
}
~~~

For larger projects, a mapping library such as MapStruct can automate much of this repetitive conversion. The important architectural idea comes first: **the API model and persistence model are separate concepts.**

## Transactions

A **transaction** is a group of database operations that should succeed or fail together.

Imagine creating a booking and reducing available capacity. If the first database operation succeeds but the second fails, you could end up with inconsistent data.

A transaction gives the database an all-or-nothing boundary.

Spring provides `@Transactional` for declaring that a method should run inside a transaction.

~~~java
@Service
public class BookingService {

    @Transactional
    public void createBooking(BookingRequest request) {
        // database operations that belong together
    }
}
~~~

For service-oriented application code, placing transaction boundaries on service methods is usually a sensible default because the service represents an application operation that may involve multiple repository calls.

The repository should normally focus on individual data-access operations rather than defining the business transaction boundary.

Transactions matter particularly when an operation reads and changes multiple related pieces of data. We will use them more when the application starts interacting with the database.

## Why layers make testing easier

Suppose the service depends directly on PostgreSQL. Testing a simple business rule would require a running database, schema setup and test data.

With a repository interface, you can use a fake.

A fake is a small test implementation that behaves predictably without the real external system.

For example:

~~~java
class FakeTaskRepository implements TaskRepository {
    private final List<Task> tasks = new ArrayList<>();

    @Override
    public List<Task> findAll() {
        return tasks;
    }

    @Override
    public Optional<Task> findById(Long id) {
        return tasks.stream()
            .filter(task -> task.getId().equals(id))
            .findFirst();
    }

    @Override
    public Task save(Task task) {
        tasks.add(task);
        return task;
    }
}
~~~

Then a unit test can create the service directly:

~~~java
TaskRepository repository = new FakeTaskRepository();
TaskService service = new TaskService(repository);

Task task = service.create("Learn testing");

assertEquals("Learn testing", task.getTitle());
~~~

No Spring server or PostgreSQL database is necessary for this test.

You can also use mocking libraries, where a mock is a programmable test double that records calls and returns configured values. The key point is the same: the service depends on an abstraction, so its business logic can be tested independently.

## Package by feature

There are several ways to organise a Spring Boot project. For our task manager, we will organise the code primarily by **feature** rather than putting every controller in one package, every service in another package, and every repository in a third package.

A feature-based structure could look like this:

~~~text
hu.softwaredevelopment.taskmanager
└── task
    ├── TaskController.java
    ├── TaskService.java
    ├── TaskRepository.java
    ├── TaskEntity.java
    ├── TaskMapper.java
    └── dto
        ├── CreateTaskRequest.java
        ├── UpdateTaskRequest.java
        └── TaskResponse.java
~~~

All code related to the task feature stays together.

As the application grows, you might have:

~~~text
task/
booking/
user/
auth/
~~~

Each feature can then contain the classes it needs.

This makes navigating a real project easier because you usually think in terms of features rather than asking, "Which package contains all services in the entire application?"

## A complete request flow

Let's put everything together.

~~~widget layered-request
~~~

A React request arrives:

~~~text
POST /api/tasks
        ↓
TaskController
        ↓
CreateTaskRequest
        ↓
TaskService
        ↓
TaskRepository
        ↓
PostgreSQL
~~~

The response travels back in the opposite direction:

~~~text
PostgreSQL
    ↓
Entity
    ↓
TaskService
    ↓
DTO
    ↓
TaskController
    ↓
JSON response
~~~

Each layer has a small, understandable responsibility.

## Common mistakes

### Putting business rules in controllers

A controller should not decide whether a task is already completed or whether a title is unique. Those rules belong in the service.

### Putting business rules in repositories

Repositories should handle data access. They should not decide what the application is allowed to do with the data.

### Constructing dependencies manually

Avoid creating repositories with `new` inside services. Let Spring inject dependencies through the constructor.

### Using field injection everywhere

Field injection hides required dependencies and makes simple unit testing harder. Prefer constructor injection.

### Creating interfaces without a reason

Interfaces are useful boundaries, but an interface for every class can add unnecessary complexity. Introduce abstractions where they provide value.

### Returning entities directly from every endpoint

Keeping DTOs separate from persistence entities gives you control over the public API and protects it from database implementation details.

### Making controllers too thin or too clever

A controller should not contain business logic, but it also should not become a second service by performing complicated transformations and decisions. Keep HTTP concerns in the controller and application rules in the service.

## The architecture we will build

The task manager now has a clear structure:

~~~text
React frontend
      ↓
REST Controller
      ↓
Service
      ↓
Repository
      ↓
PostgreSQL
~~~

The controller speaks HTTP. The service speaks application rules. The repository speaks persistence.

That separation is more than an organisational preference. It gives each part a clear responsibility, makes dependencies explicit and allows the business logic to be tested without starting the entire application.

You now have the architectural foundation for the rest of the course. In Module 6, we will introduce SQL, design the task database, map Java entities with JPA, manage schema changes with Flyway and eventually look at query performance.
takeaways: Controllers handle HTTP concerns, services contain application rules, and repositories handle data access.
Constructor injection makes dependencies explicit, keeps required dependencies immutable and simplifies unit testing.
Business rules such as task uniqueness and completion rules belong in the service layer.
DTOs and entities represent different boundaries and should not automatically be exposed as the same model.
Feature-based packages keep related task, booking or user code together as the application grows.

quiz.question: Which responsibility belongs primarily in the service layer?
options: Reading the HTTP URL
Deciding whether an already completed task can be completed again
Serialising a Java object to JSON
Reading the Authorization HTTP header
quiz.explanation: Whether an operation is allowed according to application rules is business logic, so it belongs in the service layer.

quiz.question: Why is constructor injection preferred in this course?
options: It makes Java compile without a JDK
It automatically creates database tables
It makes required dependencies explicit and makes the class easy to construct in tests
It prevents controllers from returning JSON
quiz.explanation: Constructor injection exposes the class's required dependencies and allows tests to pass a fake or mock directly to the constructor.

quiz.question: What is the main responsibility of a repository?
options: Handling HTTP status codes
Implementing React components
Applying every business rule
Reading and writing application data through the persistence layer
quiz.explanation: Repositories provide data-access operations such as finding and saving entities.

options: It marks the operations as belonging to a transaction boundary
It makes both repositories into controllers
It disables database transactions
It converts the booking into JSON
quiz.explanation: @Transactional tells Spring to execute the method within a database transaction, allowing related operations to be committed or rolled back together.

quiz.question: Why can a service that depends on a TaskRepository interface be unit tested with a fake repository?
options: Java automatically replaces PostgreSQL during every test
The service only requires the interface's contract, so another implementation can be supplied
Interfaces can only be used in tests
Spring controllers cannot use interfaces
quiz.explanation: The service depends on the repository contract rather than a specific implementation, so a test can supply a fake that implements the same interface.

exercise.title: Build a service with dependency injection
exercise.task: Complete the TaskService while keeping the provided TaskRepository interface and InMemoryTaskRepository implementation unchanged. The design mirrors the Java/Spring architecture you will build in IntelliJ IDEA: TaskService receives a TaskRepository through its constructor, which is constructor injection. Define ConflictError and NotFoundError as classes extending Error. TaskService.create(title) must trim the title, check whether a task with the same title already exists using a case-insensitive comparison, throw ConflictError("Task already exists") when it does, otherwise create { id: 0, title, done: false }, save it through the repository and return the saved task. TaskService.complete(id) must find the task through the repository, throw NotFoundError("Task not found") when it does not exist, throw ConflictError("Task is already done") when it is already done, otherwise save the task with done: true and return the saved task. The tests pass their own fake repositories to prove that the service depends only on the TaskRepository interface rather than directly on the in-memory implementation.
exercise.hint: The service should know only about TaskRepository. For create(), get all tasks through findAll() and compare titles after trimming and converting them to lowercase. For a new task, pass id: 0 to save() and let the repository assign the real ID. For complete(), use findById(), check the two error cases in order, then save a copy with done: true.
